lines: Narrator
You've seen Alaska squeezed into a tiny box on your map. But its mountains hide rock that formed near the equator, about two hundred and thirty million years ago.
Narrator
So how did a piece of the tropics end up next to the Arctic? To answer that, we have to look at what Alaska is hiding.
Narrator
And it starts with that little box.
Narrator
On most maps of the United States, Alaska sits in a corner, next to Mexico. Shrunk down, so it fits.
Chars
[big, gruff, proud, mildly offended giant] Excuse me. I don't fit in boxes.
Narrator
Because in real life, Alaska is about half the size of India. Roughly two and a half Texases.
Narrator
By the standard measure, it has more coastline than every other American state combined.
Narrator
And all that coast feeds the most valuable wild salmon fishery on Earth. In 2022, a record seventy-nine million sockeye salmon swam back into one bay.
Narrator
It holds America's northernmost point. Its westernmost point. And, technically... its easternmost point too.
Narrator
Its islands stretch so far west, they cross the hundred-and-eightieth meridian, into the Eastern Hemisphere.
Narrator
Out there, two islands sit less than four kilometres apart. One is American, one is Russian. And between them runs the date line, so from today... you can look straight into tomorrow.
Narrator

Those far western islands were even occupied in World War Two. In 1942, Japan took AT-too and KISS-kah. A year later, about thirty-five thousand US troops landed on KISS-kah... and found it empty. The garrison had slipped away weeks earlier, in the fog.
Narrator
Possibly the most awkward landing in military history.
Narrator
And up at America's northernmost town, Oot-kee-AHG-vik, the Sun sets in mid-November... and doesn't rise again for about sixty-five days.
Narrator
America bought all of this in 1867, from Russia. For less than two cents an acre.

lines: Narrator
The handover was so strange, Alaska got two Fridays in a row. It switched calendars... and sides of the date line, on the same day.
Narrator
But none of that is the secret. The secret is under the ground. Because Alaska won't sit still.
Narrator
It's the most earthquake-prone state in America. Tens of thousands of quakes a year.
Narrator
And it keeps happening. In July 2025, a magnitude seven point three quake struck off the Alaska Peninsula.
Narrator
In 1964, on Good Friday, the ground shook for about four and a half minutes. Magnitude nine point two. The second strongest earthquake ever recorded.
Narrator
Some of the coast rose by about eleven metres. Other parts sank. The map of Alaska changed in an afternoon.
Narrator
Then in 1958, in Li-TOO-yah Bay, a quake shook a mountainside of rock into the water... and the splash raced about five hundred and twenty metres up the slope opposite.
Narrator
The splash stripped the forest so cleanly, the line is still visible from space.
Narrator
That's higher than the Eiffel Tower. About seven Qutub Minaars, stacked.
Narrator
Alaska also has more than a hundred and thirty volcanoes. In 1912, one of them, No-vah-ROOP-tah, set off the biggest eruption of the twentieth century.
Narrator
It buried a whole valley in ash, which steamed for years. Explorers called it the Valley of Ten Thousand Smokes.
Narrator
Even the oil pipeline was built expecting trouble. In 2002, a huge quake shifted the ground under it about four metres sideways... and the pipeline didn't break.
Chars
[smug, metallic, unbothered engineer voice] I was literally designed for this.
Narrator
And Deh-NAH-lee, the highest mountain in North America, is still being pushed upwards. Measured from its base, it rises even more than Everest does.
Narrator
So why is Alaska shaking, erupting and rising? Because of what's sliding in from the ocean.

lines: Narrator
Just off the coast, the floor of the Pacific Ocean is moving towards Alaska, a few centimetres every year. And it dives underneath, into a trench more than seven kilometres deep.
Narrator
Think of it as a giant conveyor belt. Anything sitting on top gets delivered.
Narrator
The same belt built the Aleutian Islands, a curved chain of volcanoes stretching about nineteen hundred kilometres.
Narrator
Islands. Volcanoes. Chunks of old sea floor. When they reach Alaska, they're too light and too thick to sink. So they get scraped off... and stuck on.
Narrator
And that's what Alaska is hiding. It isn't one piece of land. It's dozens of pieces, from all over the Pacific, glued together. Geologists call them terranes.
Narrator
Remember that rock from the equator? It began as a giant pile of volcanic rock, built up from the sea floor near the equator.
Narrator
We know, because its rocks still carry fossils of warm, shallow-sea reefs. And tiny magnetic minerals, frozen in the lava, still record where it was born.
Narrator
The conveyor belt carried it thousands of kilometres north. Today, part of it forms Alaska's mountains.
Chars
[shivering, teeth chattering, sulky beach lover] Nobody told me there'd be snow.
Narrator
And here's the twist. The delivery hasn't stopped.
Narrator
Right now, another block of land is ramming into southern Alaska, pushing up some of the tallest coastal mountains on Earth.
Narrator
Alaska isn't finished. It's still arriving.
Narrator
And India knows the feeling. It drifted across an ocean too... and it's still pushing into Asia.
Chars
[big, gruff, proud, mildly offended giant] Please. No more packages.
Narrator
So next time you see Alaska squeezed into a little box on a map... remember, it's still being delivered.
Narrator
This is Bhoogol. Follow for more Geography Fun Facts.
